    Why is Persian New Year in March?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Persian New Year, or
    Nowruz, falls in March because it is astronomically aligned with the vernal equinox (spring equinox) in the Northern Hemisphere. Marking the start of spring and the renewal of nature, it occurs on the first day of the first month (Farvardin) in the Iranian calendar. 
    Key details about why it is in March: 
    • Astronomical Timing: Nowruz is calculated exactly, matching the exact moment the sun crosses the celestial equator and equalizes night and day, which occurs on March 20 or 21.
    • Symbolism of Spring: It celebrates the end of winter, symbolizing rebirth and harmony with nature.
    • Ancient Traditions:
      It is a 3,000-year-old holiday with roots in Zoroastrianism, celebrating the return of life to the world.
    • Calendar System: It marks the first day of the Iranian Solar Hijri Calendar, a year calculated from the spring equinox.
    • Cultural Significance: As the “new day,” it is widely celebrated across Central Asia, the Middle East, and beyond, with the UN recognizing March 21 as International Nowruz Day.
